problems.title: Relativistic Particle
problems.statement:
In the theory of special relativity the relation between energy $E$ and momentum $P$ or a free particle with rest mass $m_0$ is

$$E=\sqrt{p^2c^2+m_0^2c^4}=mc^2.$$

When such a particle is subject to a conservative force, the total energy of the particle, which is the sum of $\sqrt{p^2c^2+m_0^2c^4}$ and the potential energy, is conserved. If the energy of the particle is very high, the rest energy of the particle can be ignored (such a particle is called an ultra relativistic particle).

parts.statement:
consider the one dimensional motion of a very high energy particle (in which rest energy can be neglected) subject to an attractive central force of constant magnitude $f$. Suppose the particle is located at the centre of force with initial momentum $p_0$ at time $t=0$. Describe the motion of the particle by separately plotting, for at least one period of the motion: $x$ against time $t$, and momentum $p$ against space coordinate $x$. Specify the coordinates of the “turning points” in terms of given parameters $p_0$ and $f$. Indicate, with arrows, the direction of the progress of the mothon in the $(p,x)$ diagram. There may be short intervals of time during which the particle is not ultrarelativistic. However, these should be neglected.

Use Answer Sheet 1.

![](p1-answer-1)

figures.alt: Original blank Answer Sheet1, both complete coordinate axes and labels.

parts.statement:
A meson is a particle made up of two quarks. The rest mass $M$ of the meson is equal to the total energy of the two-quark system divided by $c^2$.

Consider a one-dimensional model for a meson at rest, in which the two quarks are assumed to move along the $x$-axis and attract each other with a force of constant magnitude $f$. It is assumed they can pass through each other freely. For analysis of the high energy motion of the quarks the rest mass of the quarks can be neglected. At time $t=0$ the two quarks are both at $x=0$. Show separately the motion of the two quarks graphically by a $(x,t)$ diagram and a $(p,x)$ diagram, specify the coordinates of the “turning points” in terms of $M$ and $f$, indicate the direction of the process in your $(p,x)$ diagram, and determine the maximum distance between the two quarks.

Use Answer Sheet 2.

![](p1-answer-2)

figures.alt: Original blank Answer Sheet2 with shared position-time axes, separate momentum-position axes, quark labels and maximum-distance field.

parts.statement:
The reference frame used in part 2 will be referred to as frame $S$, the Lab frame, referred to as $S$, moves in the negative $x$-direction with a constant velocity $v=0.6c$. the coordinates in the two reference frames are so chosen that the point $x=0$ in $S$ coincides with the point $x'=0$ in $S''$ at time $t=t'=0$. Plot the motion of the two quarks graphically in a $(x',t')$ diagram. Specify the coordinates of the turning points in terms of $M$, $f$ and $c$, and determine the maximum distance between the two quarks observed in Lab frame $S'$.

Use Answer Sheet 3.

The coordinates of particle observed in reference frames $S$ and $S''$ are related by the Lorentz transformation

$$\begin{cases}x'=\gamma(x+\beta ct),\\t'=\gamma\left(t+\beta\frac{x}{c}\right),\end{cases}$$

where $\beta=v/c$, $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$ and $v$ is the velocity of frame $S$ moving relative to the frame $S''$.

![](p1-answer-3)

figures.alt: Original blank Answer Sheet3 with both quark labels, complete axes and printed maximum-separation field.

parts.statement: For a meson with rest energy $Mc^2=140\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and velocity $0.60c$ relative to the Lab frame $S''$, determine its energy $E'$ in the Lab Frame $S''$.

sections.statement:
1a. Taking the force center as the origin of the space coordinate $x$ and the zero potential point, the potential energy of the particle is

$$U(x)=f\lvert x\rvert.\tag{1}$$

The total energy is

$$W=\sqrt{p^2c^2+m_0^2c^4}+f\lvert x\rvert.$$

1b. Neglecting the rest energy, we get

$$W=\lvert p\rvert c+f\lvert x\rvert,\tag{2}$$

Since $W$ is conserved throughout the motion, so we have

$$W=\lvert p\rvert c+f\lvert x\rvert=p_0c.\tag{3}$$

Let the $x$ axis be in the direction of the initial momentum of the particle,

$$\begin{aligned}pc+fx&=p_0c&&\text{when }x>0,\ p>0;\\-pc+fx&=p_0c&&\text{when }x>0,\ p<0;\\pc-fx&=p_0c&&\text{when }x<0,\ p>0;\\-pc-fx&=p_0c&&\text{when }x<0,\ p<0.\end{aligned}\tag{4}$$

The maximum distance of the particle from the origin, let it be $L$, corresponds to $p=0$. It is

$$L=p_0c/f.$$

1c. From Eq. 3 and Newton’s law

$$\frac{dp}{dt}=F=\begin{cases}-f,&x>0;\\f,&x<0;\end{cases}\tag{5}$$

we can get the speed of the particle as

$$\left\lvert\frac{dx}{dt}\right\rvert=\frac{c}{f}\left\lvert\frac{dp}{dt}\right\rvert=c,\tag{6}$$

i.e. the particle with very high energy always moves with the speed of light except that it is in the region extremely close to the points $x=\pm L$. The time for the particle to move from origin to the point $x=L$, let it be denoted by $\tau$, is

$$\tau=L/c=p_0/f.$$

So the particle moves to and for between $x=L$ and $x=-L$ with speed $c$ and period $4\tau=4p_0/f$. The relation between $x$ and $t$ is

$$\begin{aligned}x&=ct,&0&\le t\le\tau;\\x&=2L-ct,&\tau&\le t\le2\tau;\\x&=2L-ct,&2\tau&\le t\le3\tau;\\x&=ct-4L,&3\tau&\le t\le4\tau.\end{aligned}\tag{7}$$

The required answer is thus as given in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2.

![](p1-sol-fig12)

figures.alt: Original solution Figs1–2, all turning points, momentum arrows and original inconsistent L label.

sections.statement:
The total energy of the two-quark system can be expressed as

$$Mc^2=\lvert p_1\rvert c+\lvert p_2\rvert c+f\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert,\tag{8}$$

where $x_1,x_2$ are the position coordinates and $p_1,p_2$ are the momenta of quark 1 and quark 2 respectively. For the rest meson, the total momentum of the two quarks is zero and the two quarks move symmetrically in opposite directions, we have

$$p=p_1+p_2=0,\qquad p_1=-p_2,\qquad x_1=-x_2.\tag{9}$$

Let $p_0$ denote the momentum of the quark 1 when it is at $x=0$, then we have

$$Mc^2=2p_0c\qquad\text{or}\qquad p_0=Mc/2.\tag{10}$$

From Eq. 8, 9 and 10, the half of the total energy can be expressed in terms of $p_1$ and $x_1$ of quark 1:

$$p_0c=\lvert p_1\rvert c+f\lvert x_1\rvert,\tag{11}$$

just as though it is a one particle problem as in part 1 (Eq. 3) with initial momentum $p_0=Mc/2$. From the answer in part 1 we get the $(x,t)$ diagram and $(p,x)$ diagram of the motion of quark 1 as shown in Figs. 3 and 4. For quark 2 the situation is similar except that the signs are reversed for both $x$ and $p$; its $(x,t)$ and $(p,x)$ diagrams are shown in Figs. 3 and 4.

The maximum distance between the two quarks as seen from Fig. 3 is

$$d=2L=2p_0c/f=Mc^2/f.\tag{12}$$

![](p1-sol-fig34)

figures.alt: Original solution Fig3 position-time graph and both Fig4 momentum-position graphs, full labels and parameter values.

sections.statement:
The reference frame $S$ moves with a constant velocity $V=0.6c$ relative to the Lab frame $S''$ in the $x'$ axis direction, and the origins of the two frames are coincident at the beginning $(t=t'=0)$. The Lorentz transformation between these two frames is given by:

$$\begin{cases}x'=\gamma(x+\beta ct),\\t'=\gamma(t+\beta x/c),\end{cases}\tag{13}$$

where $\beta=V/c$, and $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$. With $V=0.6c$, we have $\beta=3/5$, and $\gamma=5/4$. Since the Lorenta transformation is linear, a straight line in the $(x,t)$ diagram transforms into a straight line the $(x',t')$ diagram, thus we need only to calculate the coordinates of the turning points in the frame $S'$.

For quark 1, the coordinates of the turning points in the frames $S$ and $S'$ are as follows:

$$x_1'=\gamma(x_1+\beta ct_1)=\frac54x_1+\frac34ct_1,\qquad t_1'=\gamma(t_1+\beta x_1/e)=\frac54t_1+\frac34x_1/c.$$

| Frame $S$: $x_1$ | $t_1$ | Frame $S'$: $x_1'$ | $t_1'$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $L$ | $\tau$ | $\gamma(1+\beta)L=2L$ | $\gamma(1+\beta)\tau=2\tau$ |
| $0$ | $2\tau$ | $2\gamma\beta L=\tfrac32L$ | $2\gamma\tau=\tfrac52\tau$ |
| $-L$ | $3\tau$ | $\gamma(3\beta-1)L=L$ | $\gamma(3-\beta)\tau=3\tau$ |
| $0$ | $4\tau$ | $4\gamma\beta L=3L$ | $4\gamma\tau=5\tau$ |

where $L=p_0c/f=Mc^2/2f$, $\tau=p_0/f=Mc/2f$.

For quark 2, we have

$$x_2'=\gamma(x_2+\beta ct_2)=\frac54x_2+\frac34ct_2,\qquad t_2'=\gamma(t_2+\beta x_2/c)=\frac54t_2+\frac34x_2/c.$$

| Frame $S$: $x_2$ | $t_2$ | Frame $S'$: $x_2'$ | $t_2'$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $-L$ | $\tau$ | $-\gamma(1-\beta)L=-\tfrac12L$ | $\gamma(1-\beta)\tau=\tfrac12\tau$ |
| $0$ | $2\tau$ | $2\gamma\beta L=\tfrac32L$ | $2\gamma\tau=\tfrac52\tau$ |
| $L$ | $3\tau$ | $\gamma(3\beta+1)L=\tfrac72L$ | $\gamma(3+\beta)\tau=\tfrac92\tau$ |
| $0$ | $4\tau$ | $4\gamma\beta L=3L$ | $4\gamma\tau=5\tau$ |

With the above results, the $(x',t')$ diagrams of the two quarks are shown in Fig. 5. The equations of the straight lines OA and OB are:

$$x_1'(t')=ct';\qquad0\le t'\le\gamma(1+\beta)\tau=2\tau;\tag{14a}$$

$$x_2'(t')=-ct';\qquad0\le t'\le\gamma(1-\beta)\tau=\frac12\tau.\tag{14b}$$

The distance between the two quarks attains its maximum $d'$ when $t'=\tfrac12\tau$, thus we have maximum distance

$$d'=2c\gamma(1-\beta)\tau=2\gamma(1-\beta)L=\frac{Mc^2}{2f}.\tag{15}$$

![](p1-sol-fig5)

figures.alt: Original laboratory-frame Fig5 with both quark trajectories and all turning points.

sections.statement:
It is given the meson moves with velocity $V=0.6c$ relative to the Lab frame, its energy measured in the Lab frame is

$$E'=\frac{Mc^2}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}=\frac1{0.8}\times140=175\ \mathrm{MeV}.$$

problems.title: Superconducting Magnet
problems.statement:
Super conducting magnets are widely used in laboratories. The most common form of super conducting magnets is a solenoid made of super conducting wire. The wonderful thing about a superconducting magnet is that it produces high magnetic fields without any energy dissipation due to Joule heating, since the electrical resistance of the superconducting wire becomes zero when the magnet is immersed in liquid helium at a temperature of $4.2\ \mathrm{K}$. Usually, the magnet is provided with a specially designed superconducting switch, as shown in Fig. 1. The resistance $r$ of the switch can be controlled: either $r=0$ in the superconducting state, or $r=r_n$ in the normal state. When the persistent mode, with a current circulating through the magnet and superconducting switch indefinitely. The persistent mode allows a steady magnetic field to be maintained for long periods with the external source cut off.

The details of the superconducting switch are not given in Fig. 1. It is usually a small length of superconducting wire wrapped with a heater wire and suitably thermally insulated from the liquid helium bath. On being heated, the temperature of the superconducting wire increases and it reverts to the resistive normal state. The typical value of $r_n$ is a few ohms. Here we assume it to be $5\ \Omega$. The inductance of a superconducting magnet depends on its size; assume it be $10\ \mathrm{H}$ for the magnet in Fig. 1. The total current $I$ can be changed by adjusting the resistance $R$.

**This problem will be graded by the plots only!**

The arrows denote the positive direction of $I$, $I_1$ and $I_2$.

![](p2-circuit)

figures.alt: Original Fig1 complete superconducting magnet circuit, heater-switch annotation, current arrows and liquid-helium note.

parts.statement:
If the total current $I$ and the resistance $r$ of the superconducting switch are controlled to vary with time in the way shown in Figs. 2a and 2b respectively, and assuming the currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ flowing through the magnet and the switch respectively are equal at the beginning (Fig. 2c and Fig. 2d), how do they vary with time from $t_1$ to $t_4$? Plot your answer in Fig. 2c and Fig. 2d.

![](p2-fig2)

figures.alt: Original all four Fig2 graph panels, complete axes, prescribed I/r and initial I1/I2 segments.

parts.statement:
Suppose the power switch $K$ is turned on at time $t=0$ when $r=0$, $I_1=0$ and $R=7.5\ \Omega$, and the total current $I$ is $0.5\ \mathrm{A}$. With $K$ kept closed, the resistance $r$ of the superconducting switch is varied in he way shown in Fig. 3b. Plot the corresponding time dependences of $I$, $I_1$ and $I_2$ in Figs. 3a, 3c and 3d respectively.

![](p2-fig3)

figures.alt: Original complete four Fig3 blank/current-resistance graph panels and all minute tick labels.

parts.statement:
Only small currents, less than $0.5\ \mathrm{A}$, are allowed to flow through the superconducting switch when it is in the normal state, with larger currents the switch will be burnt out. Suppose the superconducting magnet is operated in a persistent mode, i.e. $I=0$, and $I_1=i_1$ (e.g. $20\ \mathrm{A}$), $I_2=-i_1$, as shown in Fig. 4, from $t=0$ to $t=3\ \mathrm{min}$. If the experiment is to be stopped by reducting the current through the magnet to zero, how would you do it? This has to be done in several operation steps. Plot the corresponding changes of $I$, $r$, $I_1$ and $I_2$ in Fig. 4.

![](p2-fig4)

figures.alt: Original four Fig4 panels including negative20A I2 level, complete axes and time scales.

parts.statement:
Suppose the magnet is operated in a persistent mode with a persistent current of $20\ \mathrm{A}$ ($t=0$ to $t=3\ \mathrm{min}$. See Fig. 5). How would you change it to a persistent mode with a current of 30a? plot your answer in Fig. 5.

![](p2-fig5abc)

![](p2-fig5d)

figures.alt: Original Fig5a–c graph panels, complete20A/30A levels and minute ticks.
Original Fig5d I2 panel continued on next native page, including negative20A/30A levels.

sections.statement:
For $t=t_1$ to $t_3$:

Since $r=0$, the voltage across the magnet $V_M=L\,dI_1/dt=0$, therefore,

$$I_1=I_1(t_1)=\frac12I_0;\qquad I_2=I-I_1=I-\frac12I_0.$$

For $t=t_3$ to $t_4$:

Since $I_2=0$ at $t=t_3$, and $I$ is kept at $\tfrac12I_0$ after $t=t_3$, $V_M=I_2r_n=0$, therefore, $I_1$ and $I_2$ will not change.

$$I_1=\frac12I_0;\qquad I_2=0.$$

These results are shown in Fig. 6.

![](p2-sol-fig6)

figures.alt: Original complete solution Fig6a–d including I2 negative segment.

sections.statement:
For $t=0$ to $t=1\ \mathrm{min}$:

Since $r=0$, $V_M=L\,dI_1/dt=0$,

$$I_1=I_1(0)=0,\qquad I_2=I-I_1=0.5\ \mathrm{A}.$$

At $t=1\ \mathrm{min}$, $r$ suddenly jumps from $0$ to $r_n$, $I$ will drop from $E/R$ to $E/(R+r_n)$ instantaneously, because $I_1$ can not change abruptly due to the inductance of the magnet coil. For $E/R=0.5\ \mathrm{A}$, $R=7.5\ \Omega$ and $R_n=5\ \Omega$, $I$ will drop to $0.3\ \mathrm{A}$.

For $t=1\ \mathrm{min}$ to $2\ \mathrm{min}$:

$I$, $I_1$ and $I_2$ gradually approach their steady values:

$$I=\frac ER=0.5\ \mathrm{A},\qquad I_1=I=0.5\ \mathrm{A},\qquad I_2=0.$$

The time constant

$$\tau=\frac{L(R+r_n)}{Rr_n}.$$

When $L=10\ \mathrm{H}$, $R=7.5\ \Omega$ and $r_n=5\ \Omega$, $\tau=3\ \mathrm{sec}$.

For $t=2\ \mathrm{min}$ to $3\ \mathrm{min}$:

Since $r=0$, $I_1$ and $I_2$ will not change, that is

$$I_1=0.5\ \mathrm{A}\quad\text{and}\quad I_2=0.$$

![](p2-sol-fig7ab)

![](p2-sol-fig7cd)

figures.alt: Original solution Fig7a/b with current jump/transient and resistance pulse.
Original solution Fig7c/d continued on native next page, complete rise/decay curves.

sections.statement:
The operation steps are:

**First step**

Turn on power switch $K$, and increase the total current $I$ to $20\ \mathrm{A}$, i.e. equal to $I_1$.

Since the superconducting switch is in the state $r=0$, so that $V_M=L\,dI_1/dt=0$, that is, $I_1$ can not change and $I_2$ increases by $20\ \mathrm{A}$, in other words, $I_2$ changes from $-20\ \mathrm{A}$ to zero.

**Second step**

Switch $r$ from $0$ to $r_n$.

**Third step**

Gradually reduce $I$ to zero while keeping $I_2<0.5\ \mathrm{A}$; since $I_2=V_M/r_n$ and $V_m=L\,dI_1/dt$, when $L=10\ \mathrm{H}$, $r_n=5\ \Omega$, the requirement $I_2<0.5\ \mathrm{A}$ corresponds to $dI_1/dt<0.25\ \mathrm{A/sec}$, that is, a drop of $<15\ \mathrm{A}$ in $1\ \mathrm{min}$. In Fig. 8 $dI/dt\sim0.1\ \mathrm{A/sec}$ and $dI_1/dt$ is around this value too, so the requirement has been fulfilled.

**Final step**

Switch $r$ to zero when $V_M=0$ and turn off the power switch $K$. These results are shown in Fig. 8.

![](p2-sol-fig8abc)

![](p2-sol-fig8d)

figures.alt: Original solution Fig8a–c, all operation stages and levels.
Original solution Fig8d continued on next page, full I2 rise from negative20A.

sections.statement:
**First step and second step** are the same as that in part 3, resulting in $I_2=0$.

**Third step** Increase $I$ by $10\ \mathrm{A}$ to $30\ \mathrm{A}$ with a rate subject to the requirement $I_2<0.5\ \mathrm{A}$.

**Fourth step** Switch $r$ to zero when $V_M=0$.

**Fifth step** Reduce $I$ to zero, $I_1=30\ \mathrm{A}$ will not change because $V_M$ is zero. $I_2=I-I_1$ will change to $-30\ \mathrm{A}$. The current flowing through the magnet is thus closed by the superconducting switch.

**Final step** Turn off the power switch $K$. The magnet is operating in the persistent mode.

These results are shown in Fig. 9.

![](p2-sol-fig9)

figures.alt: Original solution Fig9a–d with every graph panel, operation times and negative30A level.

sections.title: Grading Scheme
sections.statement:
Part 1 — 2 points:

0.5 point for each of $I_1$, $I_2$ from $t=t_1$ to $t_3$ and $I_1$, $I_2$ from $t=t_3$ to $t_4$.

Part 2 — 3 points:

0.3 point for each of $I$, $I_1$, $I_2$ from $t=0$ to $1\ \mathrm{min}$, $I$, $I_1$, $I_2$ at $t=1\ \mathrm{min}$, and $I_0$, $I_1$, $I_2$ from $t=1$ to $2\ \mathrm{min}$;

0.2 point for each of $I$, $I_1$, and $I_2$ from $t=2$ to $3\ \mathrm{min}$.

Part 3 — 2 points:

0.25 point for each section in Fig. 8 from $t=3$ to $9\ \mathrm{min}$, 8 sections in total.

Part 4 — 3 points:

0.25 point for each section in Fig. 9 from $t=3$ to $12\ \mathrm{min}$, 12 sections in total.

problems.title: Collision of Discs with Surface Friction
problems.statement:
A homogeneous disc A of mass $m$ and radius $R_A$ moves translationally on a smooth horizontal $x$-$y$ plane in the $x$ direction with a velocity $V$ (see the figure on the next page). The center of the disk is at a distance $b$ from the $x$-axis. It collides with a stationary homogeneous disc B whose center is initially located at the origin of the coordinate system. The disc B has the same mass and the same thickness as A, but its radius is $R_B$. It is assumed that the velocities of the discs at their point of contact, in the direction perpendicular to the line joining their centers, are equal after the collision. It is also assumed that the magnitudes of the relative velocities of the discs along the line joining their centers are the same before and after the collision.

![](p3-question)

figures.alt: Original question geometry, both discs, impact parameter b, velocity V and complete x/y axes.

parts.statement: For such a collision determine the $X$ and $Y$ components of the velocities of the two discs after the collision, i.e. $V'_{AX}$, $V'_{AY}$, $V'_{BX}$ and $V'_{BY}$ in terms of $m$, $R_A$, $R_B$, $V$ and $b$.
Determine the kinetic energies $E'_A$ for disc A and $E'_B$ for disc B after the collision in terms of $m$, $R_A$, $R_B$, $V$ and $b$.

sections.statement:
When disc A collides with disc B, let $n$ be the unit vector along the normal to the surfaces at the point of contact and $t$ be the tangential unit vector as shown in the figure. Let $\varphi$ be the angle between $n$ and the $x$ axis. Then we have

$$b=(R_A+R_B)\sin\varphi.$$

The momentum components of A and B along $n$ and $t$ before collision are:

$$mV_{An}=mV\cos\varphi,\quad mV_{Bn}=0,\qquad mV_{At}=mV\sin\varphi,\quad mV_{Bt}=0.$$

Denote the corresponding momentum components of A and B after collision by $mV'_{An}$, $mV'_{Bn}$, $mV'_{At}$, and $mV'_{Bt}$. Let $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ be the angular velocities of A and B about the axes through their centers after collision, and $I_A$ and $I_B$ be their corresponding moments of intertia. Then,

$$I_A=\frac12mR_A^2,\qquad I_B=\frac12mR_B^2.$$

The conservation of momentum gives

$$mV\cos\varphi=mV'_{An}+mV'_{Bn},\tag{1}$$

$$mV\sin\varphi=mV'_{At}+mV'_{tn}.\tag{2}$$

The conservation of angular momentum about the axis through O gives

$$mVb=mV'_{At}(R_A+R_B)+I_A\omega_A+I_B\omega_B.\tag{3}$$

The impulse of the friction force exerted on B during collision will cause a momentum change of $mV'_{At}$ along $t$ and produces an angular momentum $I_B\omega_B$ simultaneously. They are related by.

$$mV'_{Bt}R_b=I_B\omega_B.\tag{4}$$

![](p3-solution)

During the collision at the point of contact A and B acquires the same tangential velocities, so we have

$$V'_{At}-\omega_AR_A=V'_{Bt}-\omega_BR_B.\tag{5}$$

It is given that the magnitudes of the relative velocities along the normal direction of the two discs before and after collision are equal, i.e.

$$V\cos\varphi=V'_{Bn}-V'_{An}.\tag{6}$$

From Eqs. 1 and 6 we get

$$V'_{An}=0,\qquad V'_{Bn}=V\cos\varphi.$$

From Eqs. 2 to 5, we get

$$V'_{At}=\frac56V\sin\varphi,\qquad V'_{Bt}=\frac16V\sin\varphi,\qquad\omega_A=\frac{V\sin\varphi}{3R_A},\qquad\omega_B=\frac{V\sin\varphi}{3R_B}.$$

The $x$ and $y$ components of the velocities after collision are:

$$V'_{Ax}=V'_{An}\cos\varphi+V'_{At}\sin\varphi=\frac{5Vb^2}{6(R_A+R_B)^2},\tag{7}$$

$$V'_{Ay}=-V'_{An}\sin\varphi+V'_{At}\cos\varphi=\frac{5Vb\sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2-b^2}}{6(R_A+R_B)^2},\tag{8}$$

$$V'_{Bx}=V'_{Bn}\cos\varphi+V'_{Bt}\sin\varphi=\left[1-\frac{5b^2}{6(R_A+R_B)^2}\right],\tag{9}$$

$$V'_{By}=-V'_{Bn}\sin\varphi+V'_{Bt}\cos\varphi=-\frac{5Vb\sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2-b^2}}{6(R_A+R_B)^2}.\tag{10}$$

figures.alt: Original contact geometry with all normal/tangential arrows, angle phi and both disc radii.

sections.statement:
After the collision, the kinetic energy of disc A is

$$E'_A=\frac12m\left({V'_{Ax}}^2+{V'_{Ay}}^2\right)+\frac12I_A\omega_A^2=\frac{3mV^2b^2}{8(R_A+R_B)^2},\tag{11}$$

while the kinetic energy of disc B is

$$E'_B=\frac12m\left({V'_{Bx}}^2+{V'_{By}}^2\right)+\frac12I_B\omega_B^2=\frac12mV^2\left[1-\frac{11b^2}{12(R_A+R_B)^2}\right].\tag{12}$$
